feedbackItems.pattern: Missing root reassignment in recursive remove
feedbackItems.explanation: testRemoveReturnValue() and testRemove() both failed from run 13 through run 19 and were fixed at run 20, requiring 7 runs. The run 20 diff shows two key changes. First, `root.remove(element, bC)` was updated to `root = root.remove(element, bC)`, and similarly for insert. When remove() returns a new subtree root (for example, after deleting the root node itself), the tree's root field must be reassigned to capture this return value; otherwise, the root field continues pointing to the old, now-detached node. Second, the two-children removal case was modified: the predecessor's left child was being unconditionally reassigned, but the fix added a guard (`if (left != predecessor)`) to handle the edge case where the in-order predecessor is the immediate left child. The change from `if` to `else if` in the comparison chain also corrected a logic error where multiple branches could execute for the same node, causing incorrect tree structure after removal.
nextSteps: This pointer-replacement pattern recurs in EditorTrees Milestone 3, where delete(int pos) uses the same three-case removal logic but must also rebalance; practice writing remove so that every recursive call returns the (possibly new) subtree root and the caller always reassigns its child pointer to that returned value.

For the two-children case in BST removal, trace through the scenario where the in-order predecessor is the direct left child versus a deeper right-descendant. The guard condition on predecessor reassignment prevents accidentally detaching the left subtree when the predecessor has no right children.

Use `else if` chains (not independent `if` statements) when the comparison outcomes are mutually exclusive. Independent `if` blocks can cause a node that was just identified as equal to also fall into the greater-than or less-than branch if data changes mid-method.

feedbackItems.pattern: Missing root reassignment in insert broke size tracking
feedbackItems.explanation: testSize() failed at runs 13-15 and was fixed at run 16, requiring 3 runs. The diff shows a single one-line change: `root.insert(o, bC)` became `root = root.insert(o, bC)`. Without reassigning root to the return value of insert(), the very first insertion into an empty tree (where root is NULL_NODE) would call insert on NULL_NODE, which returns a new Node, but that new Node was never stored back into root. Consequently, the tree remained empty, and size() returned 0 regardless of how many elements were inserted. This same bug affected multiple test categories simultaneously, since insert is the foundation for populating the tree.
nextSteps: The concept of recursive size computation, where size(node) = 1 + size(left) + size(right), directly underpins the rank invariant in EditorTrees, where each node stores the size of its left subtree. Practice computing size both recursively and by maintaining a cached count updated during insert/remove.

When using a sentinel NULL_NODE pattern, remember that NULL_NODE.insert() must return a new node, and the caller must capture that return value. Trace through the empty-tree insertion case on paper to verify the root pointer gets updated.

feedbackItems.pattern: Incorrect stack element type and traversal logic in pre-order iterator
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed across 11 runs (runs 18 through 28). The initial failure at run 18 returned null instead of the expected value 6, indicating the iterator's traversal logic was incomplete. By run 19, the error shifted to hasNext() incorrectly returning true when it should return false, which persisted unchanged through runs 20, 21, and 22. The root cause, visible in the run 29 diff, was twofold: the stack was storing data values (Stack<T>) instead of nodes (Stack<Node>), and the hasNext() method was checking node references (root != NULL_NODE || root.left != NULL_NODE || root.right != NULL_NODE) instead of simply checking whether the stack was empty. The fix changed the stack type to Stack<Node>, pushed the root node during initialization only if it was not NULL_NODE, rewrote hasNext() to return !stck.isEmpty(), and restructured next() to pop a node and push its right then left children. This correctly implements the standard stack-based pre-order traversal pattern.
nextSteps: The stack-based pre-order traversal pattern recurs in EditorTrees toString(), which requires O(N) in-order traversal; internalize the general approach of pushing nodes (not data) onto a stack and letting the stack drive hasNext() so you can adapt it to any traversal order.

Practice converting between pre-order, in-order, and post-order stack-based iterators by hand: pre-order pushes right then left after popping, while in-order pushes all left descendants first. Understanding these differences will help with HW6's preOrderInOrderBuild problem.

When implementing any iterator, keep the invariant simple: hasNext() should check one condition (e.g., stack emptiness), and next() should be the only method that modifies state. Avoid duplicating traversal logic between the two methods.

diffs.label: Run 29 — BinarySearchTree.java
before: return root != NULL_NODE || root.left != NULL_NODE || root.right != NULL_NODE;
after: Node node = stck.pop();  // visit this node
// push right first so left is popped/peeked first (LIFO)
diffs.note: Changed stack type from Stack<T> to Stack<Node>, rewrote hasNext() to check stack emptiness instead of node references, and restructured next() to push children nodes, fixing the pre-order traversal logic.

feedbackItems.pattern: Null iterator return followed by incorrect hasNext() state management
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed across 9 runs (runs 30 through 38). The initial failure at run 30 was a NullPointerException when calling hasNext(), indicating the iterator method was returning null rather than an iterator object. The in-order iterator requires a different initialization strategy than pre-order: rather than just pushing the root, it must push all left-spine nodes onto the stack so that the smallest element is on top. The test was ultimately fixed at run 39, likely by correctly initializing the stack with the leftmost path and, in next(), pushing the right child's left spine after popping.
nextSteps: The in-order iterator pattern directly parallels EditorTrees toString(), which must traverse nodes in rank order at O(N). Compare your pre-order and in-order iterators side by side to solidify the difference: pre-order processes a node immediately upon popping and pushes right then left; in-order defers processing until all left descendants are stacked. This distinction is tested on Exam 3.

feedbackItems.pattern: Confused Node vs. data parameter in recursive insert causing NullPointerException
feedbackItems.explanation: Both testInsertReturnValueString() and testInsertStrings() failed across runs 11 through 13 due to the same underlying bugs in the insert method. At run 11, a NullPointerException occurred because the insert helper received a Node object but compared it against NULL_NODE (a sentinel node, not null), and the constructor call new Node(node.data) was fragile when node references were confused. Run 12 fixed the null pointer issue but left ordering broken. Run 13 fixed integer ordering but strings still failed, likely because compareTo() was being checked against the literal value 1 instead of using < 0 and > 0. The run 14 diff shows the comprehensive fix: the method signature changed from accepting a Node parameter to accepting raw data (T ndata), the base case changed from checking node == NULL_NODE to this == NULL_NODE (correctly detecting when recursion has reached a leaf position), and the comparison logic was corrected. nextSteps: The recursive descent-and-return pattern used here (where each recursive call returns the updated subtree root) recurs in EditorTrees add(char, int); practice writing insert helpers where the parameter is the data to insert and 'this' is the current tree node, returning the possibly-new subtree root.
Always use compareTo() with < 0, == 0, and > 0 rather than checking for specific values like 1 or -1. The Comparable contract only guarantees the sign of the return value, not its magnitude.

When designing recursive Node methods, keep a clear distinction between the data being passed down (the value to insert) and the structural context (the current node, accessed via 'this'). Mixing these two concepts is a common source of NullPointerExceptions in tree code.

feedbackItems.pattern: Multiple pointer-update bugs in remove helper across all three cases
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed at runs 42 and 43 as part of a group of 3 failing remove tests. The run 44 diff reveals five distinct bugs that were fixed simultaneously. First, the outer remove call was not reassigning root (root.remove(...) instead of root = root.remove(...)), so removing the root node had no effect on the tree. Second, the one-child case returned 'this' instead of 'right' when the left child was NULL_NODE, failing to bypass the removed node. Third, the two-children case called searchLeft(root) instead of searchLeft(left), searching the wrong subtree for the in-order predecessor. Fourth, the subsequent removal of the predecessor was performed on the right subtree instead of the left. Fifth, the searchLeft helper traversed left (node = node.left) instead of right (node = node.right), so it found the minimum of the left subtree rather than the maximum (the actual in-order predecessor). All five fixes were necessary together to make remove work correctly.
nextSteps: The three-case remove logic (leaf, one child, two children with in-order predecessor/successor swap) recurs directly in EditorTrees Milestone 3 delete(int pos), which adds AVL rebalancing on top. Solidify your understanding of which subtree to search and which child pointer to update during the swap-and-delete step.

Practice the pointer-replacement pattern: every recursive remove helper must return the updated subtree root so the parent can reassign its child pointer. feedbackItems.pattern: Incomplete iterator returning null
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed from run 12 through run 19. At run 19, iterator() was modified to return null, which caused runtime errors. An in-order BST iterator requires maintaining traversal state between calls to next(). The standard stack-based approach initializes by pushing all left-spine nodes onto a Stack, then each call to next() pops the top node, records its value, and pushes the left spine of that node's right child. This yields elements in sorted order without building an intermediate list, making it O(h) space where h is the tree height.
nextSteps: In-order traversal is foundational for EditorTrees toString() and appears on Exams 2 and 3; implement the stack-based iterator by creating an inner class with a Stack<BSTNode> field, pushing all left children from the root in the constructor, and in next() popping the top node then pushing the left spine of its right child.
Implement hasNext() by checking whether the stack is empty. This pairs naturally with the stack-based approach since an empty stack means all nodes have been visited.
Test your iterator on a small tree (e.g., 5 nodes) by manually tracing which nodes get pushed and popped to verify the in-order sequence before running the full test suite.

feedbackItems.pattern: Unimplemented toString returning null
feedbackItems.explanation: The toString() method has returned null across all 42 runs, indicating it was never completed. The code diffs show multiple attempts to build a string representation (runs 20, 22, 23) where the code iterated over the bucket array using a StringBuilder, appending node data and "null" terminators. However, each attempt was commented out shortly after being added. Run 20 commented out the entire loop body. Run 22 changed the loop bound from this.size() to this.capacity and the null-check from NULL_NODE to null, but run 23 then commented out the inner while-loop again. The core issue is that toString() for a hash set should not dump the internal table structure; it should collect all stored string values and format them as a bracketed, comma-separated list (e.g., "[alpha, beta, gamma]"). The approach visible in the diffs, which printed bucket indices and chain traversals, was building a debug-style dump rather than the expected set representation.
nextSteps: Implement toString() by iterating over every bucket (index 0 to capacity-1), walking each chain to collect stored string values into a list, then joining them with ", " inside square brackets. An empty set should return "[]".
Use a StringBuilder and a boolean or counter to handle comma placement: append a comma before each element except the first, or build a list of all elements first and use String.join(", ", list).
Verify that your chain traversal skips sentinel/dummy head nodes if your linked list uses them, so you only collect actual data values.

feedbackItems.pattern: Rehash logic never implemented
feedbackItems.explanation: This test has failed across all 42 runs. The rehash category requires that when the load factor (size / capacity) reaches a threshold, the table doubles its capacity and redistributes all existing elements into the new, larger array. The code diffs show extensive work on add() and the hash-index computation (runs 8, 10, 11, 12, 16), but none of these changes introduced a load-factor check or a rehash method. The changes focused on fixing the hash code's modular arithmetic (handling negative hash values, correcting the loop bound in stringHashCode from length()-1 to length(), and adjusting the index calculation), which were necessary for basic add functionality. However, the add() method never gained a conditional check before or after insertion to compare size against the load-factor threshold and trigger a resize. This concept reappears on Exam 3, where you will need to calculate how many adds trigger a rehash given a specific capacity and load-factor threshold, and then diagram the redistribution of items into a doubled table.
nextSteps: At the end of your add() method (after incrementing size), check whether (double) size / capacity exceeds your load-factor threshold. If it does, call a rehash helper that: (1) saves a reference to the old array, (2) creates a new array of double the capacity, (3) updates the capacity field, (4) re-inserts every element from the old array by recomputing each element's bucket index using the new capacity.

During rehash, iterate over every bucket in the old array and walk each chain to extract stored strings. For each string, compute stringHashCode(s) % newCapacity to find its new bucket, then insert it at the head of that bucket's chain.

Test your rehash by adding elements one at a time and checking that the capacity doubles at the correct count. With capacity 5 and load factor threshold 2.0, the 11th add should trigger a resize to capacity 10.

To make that reasoning testable on your own implementation, add a new method `public int rehashCount()` to StringHashSet that returns how many rehashes have occurred since construction. hints: Add a private int field initialized to 0 — e.g. `private int mRehashCount = 0;` — and a one-line public getter that returns it. The field tracks lifetime rehash count, not the count since the last clear().

feedbackItems.pattern: Iterator method returns null, never implemented
feedbackItems.explanation: The iterator() method has returned null across all 42 runs, causing testIteratorDifferentReturns, testIteratorNextHasNext, testIteratorNoSuchElementException, and testIteratorConcurrentModificationException to all fail with the same root cause. No code diffs show any attempt to create an Iterator inner class or return an Iterator object. Implementing an iterator for a chained hash set requires a stateful object that tracks two positions: the current bucket index in the array and the current node within that bucket's linked list. The hasNext()/next()/NoSuchElementException contract implemented here is the same pattern used in every iterable collection, including EditorTrees and graph traversals in future assignments.
nextSteps: Create an inner class (e.g., StringHashSetIterator) that implements Iterator<String>. It needs two fields: a bucket index (int) and a current node reference. In the constructor, advance the bucket index to the first non-empty bucket so that hasNext() can simply check whether the current node holds data.

For next(), return the current node's data, then advance the node pointer to node.next. If node.next is the end of the chain, increment the bucket index until you find another non-empty bucket or exhaust the array. If hasNext() is false when next() is called, throw NoSuchElementException.

For concurrent modification detection, store a modCount field in the hash set that increments on every add, remove, or clear. In the iterator constructor, snapshot this value as expectedModCount. feedbackItems.pattern: Stack push-order reversal causing incorrect traversal
feedbackItems.explanation: The pre-order iterator was first implemented around run 9 but produced incorrect traversal order, causing assertion failures from run 9 through run 16. The error at run 13 flipped from 'expected false but got true' to 'expected true but got false,' indicating changes to the traversal logic. The code diff at run 17 reveals the core fix: the original code pushed the left child before the right child onto the stack, but since a stack is LIFO, this caused the left subtree to be visited after the right subtree, reversing the expected pre-order (root, left, right) sequence. The fix swapped the push order so that the right child is pushed first and the left child second, ensuring left is popped (and thus visited) before right. The diff also shows the addition of a NoSuchElementException check when hasNext() is false, which is proper iterator contract behavior.
nextSteps: Pre-order traversal understanding is tested directly in EditorTrees toString() and in HW6's preOrderInOrderBuild, where you must know exactly what information pre-order encodes (root visited first, then left subtree, then right subtree). When implementing stack-based pre-order, always remember: push right before left so that left is popped first.

For any stack-based tree traversal, trace through a small 3-node tree by hand before coding. Write down the stack contents after each push/pop to verify the visit order matches the expected traversal.
Always include the NoSuchElementException guard in iterator next() methods; this is part of the Java Iterator contract and will be expected in future assignments involving custom iterators.

feedbackItems.pattern: ClassCastException from generic array creation, resolved by ArrayList-backed approach
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed across many runs, first appearing at run 26 and not passing until run 55. The semantic context at run 51 identifies the specific error: a ClassCastException when attempting to cast Object[] to Comparable[]. This is a classic Java generics pitfall; due to type erasure, you cannot create a generic array (new T[]) at runtime, and casting Object[] to a parameterized type fails. The student worked on this across runs 51-55, and the final diff at run 55 shows the solution: the code builds an ArrayList<T> via the already-working toArrayList() method, then calls list.toArray() which returns Object[]. This avoids the unsafe cast entirely. The 37 added lines suggest the toArray() method was written fresh or rewritten from scratch along with supporting documentation.
nextSteps: Understand why Java generics and arrays do not mix well: type erasure means T is replaced by Object at runtime, so new T[] is illegal and casting Object[] to T[] causes ClassCastException. The pattern of collecting into an ArrayList<T> and then calling toArray() is a standard workaround. This same in-order collection pattern appears in EditorTrees toString(), which must gather characters in O(N) via in-order traversal.

If you ever need a typed array (e.g., Comparable[]), the approach is to use Array.newInstance(componentType, size) or accept an array parameter like the overloaded toArray(T[] a) in Java's Collection interface. For this assignment, returning Object[] via ArrayList.toArray() is the simplest correct solution.
When you encounter ClassCastException in generic code, check whether you are casting arrays or creating arrays with a generic type parameter; these are almost always the cause.

feedbackItems.pattern: Repeated regressions in in-order iterator traversal order
feedbackItems.explanation: The in-order iterator test experienced multiple regression cycles. It first broke at run 11 as part of a 6-test regression, remained broken through runs 18-21 with the error oscillating between different assertion failures (such as 'expected 1 but got 6' at run 21 and a different assertion at run 20), and was not fixed until run 24. The regression at run 18 occurred right after the pre-order iterator fix at run 17, suggesting that changes to one iterator's code affected the other, possibly because they shared data structures or were defined in the same inner class scope. The oscillating error messages across runs indicate adjustments to the traversal logic that kept producing incorrect visit order. The in-order iterator requires visiting the leftmost node first, then the parent, then the right subtree, which when implemented with a stack means you must push all left descendants initially and after each right-child step.
nextSteps: In-order traversal with a stack follows a specific pattern: (1) push all left descendants of the current node onto the stack during initialization, (2) on each next() call, pop the top node as the current value, then if it has a right child, push that right child and all of its left descendants. This pattern recurs in EditorTrees toString() which must perform O(N) in-order traversal.

When you have multiple iterator implementations (in-order, pre-order) in the same class, ensure they use separate inner classes or at minimum separate stack instances. A change to one iterator's next() logic should not affect the other; if it does, check for shared mutable state.

To debug traversal order issues, insert a small known tree (e.g., values 1, 3, 5 forming a simple 3-node BST) and print the stack contents at each step of next(). Compare the sequence of popped values against the expected in-order output.

feedbackItems.pattern: Incorrect recursive pointer reassignment in remove
feedbackItems.explanation: This test, along with testRemove, failed across runs 82-87. The initial remove implementation at run 82 had two core issues: (1) the recursive delete calls did not reassign the return value back to the left/right child pointer (e.g., `right.delete(element, bc)` instead of `right = right.delete(element, bc)`), and (2) the predecessor's subtree was incorrectly reattached using `this.left.right = predecessor.left` instead of `this.left = predecessor.left`. Run 83 introduced a NullPointerException. By run 87, the fix changed the recursive calls to `left = left.delete(element, bc)` and `right = right.delete(element, bc)`, and fixed the predecessor reattachment to `this.left = predecessor.left`. In a BST remove using the NULL_NODE sentinel pattern, every recursive call must return the (possibly updated) subtree root, and the parent must capture that return value to maintain correct tree structure.
nextSteps: This pointer-replacement-on-return pattern recurs in EditorTrees Milestone 3, where delete(int pos) uses the same three-case removal logic but adds AVL rebalancing on the way back up. Practice writing remove so that every recursive call returns the new subtree root and the caller always reassigns: left = left.delete(...), right = right.delete(...).

Review the two-children removal case carefully: after finding the in-order predecessor, you must copy its data into the current node, then recursively delete the predecessor's value from the left subtree. The left subtree pointer must be updated with the result of that recursive deletion.

Test remove with trees of varying shapes: a left-only chain, a right-only chain, a balanced tree, and cases where the node to remove is the root. Each exercises a different combination of the leaf, one-child, and two-children cases.

feedbackItems.pattern: Incorrect stack push targets and hasNext logic in pre-order iterator
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed across runs 11-41 before passing at run 42. The error progression shows: initially hasNext() returned true when it should have returned false (run 11), then returned false when it should have returned true (run 14), then the iterator produced extra elements (run 15, expected 5 but got 6). The root cause across these runs involved two issues. First, the next() method was pushing the node itself (`stack.push(n)`) back onto the stack instead of pushing its children (`stack.push(n.right)` and `stack.push(n.left)`), which caused incorrect traversal. Second, the hasNext() method toggled between `!stack.isEmpty()` and `stack.peek() != NULL_NODE`, with the correct solution combining both checks: `!stack.isEmpty() && stack.peek() != NULL_NODE`. The fix at run 42 changed the push targets to `n.right` and `n.left` (pushing right first so left is processed first), wrapped next() in a try-catch for proper exception handling, and switched hasNext() to use the peek-based check.
nextSteps: The pre-order traversal pattern, where you process the current node then push right-child-first and left-child-second, is foundational for EditorTrees toString() and for exam questions requiring you to predict traversal output from a given tree. Practice implementing all three iterative traversals (pre, in, post) using an explicit stack to solidify the push order for each.

For hasNext() with a NULL_NODE sentinel, always guard against both an empty stack and a NULL_NODE on top. The combined check `!stack.isEmpty() && stack.peek() != NULL_NODE` prevents EmptyStackException while correctly detecting traversal completion.
When debugging iterator issues, trace through a small tree (3-5 nodes) by hand, writing out the stack contents after each next() call. This makes push-target errors immediately visible.

feedbackItems.pattern: EmptyStackException evolving to NoSuchElementException in in-order iterator
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed across runs 49-73, with the error evolving from EmptyStackException to NoSuchElementException. The in-order iterator is more complex than pre-order because you cannot simply pop-and-process; you must first descend to the leftmost node before returning any value. The initial EmptyStackException (run 49) indicates the stack was being emptied prematurely, likely because the iterator was popping without properly pushing successors. The shift to NoSuchElementException (run 51) indicates the hasNext()/next() interaction was adjusted but the traversal logic still did not correctly handle moving to the in-order successor. The fix at run 74 shows a significant restructuring: the old approach tried to peek at the left child of the top-of-stack and manage a complex conditional, while the corrected version simplified to popping a node, then pushing its right child and left descendants. The hasNext() was also corrected from `return true` (which caused infinite iteration) to `!stack.isEmpty() && stack.peek() != NULL_NODE`.
nextSteps: The in-order iterator pattern directly parallels EditorTrees toString(), which must perform an O(N) in-order traversal. The standard stack-based in-order algorithm is: (1) in the constructor, push all left-spine nodes; (2) in next(), pop a node, record its value, then push the right child followed by all of that child's left descendants. Master this pattern as it recurs throughout the course.

When hasNext() unconditionally returns true, the iterator will never terminate, causing tests to hang or throw exceptions when the stack empties during next(). Always tie hasNext() to actual stack state, not a hardcoded value.

Trace the in-order iterator on a 5-node balanced BST by hand: write out the stack after the constructor, then after each next() call. Verify that elements come out in sorted order and that the stack is empty exactly when all nodes have been visited.

feedbackItems.pattern: Incomplete two-children removal case with missing subtree cleanup
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed across runs 82-94, persisting longer than the simpler testRemove and testRemoveReturnValue tests. While those tests passed by runs 85 and 87 respectively, testRemoveAdvanced continued to fail because it exercises more complex removal scenarios, particularly the two-children case where the in-order predecessor must be found, its data copied to the current node, and then the predecessor must be recursively deleted from the left subtree. The code diff at run 95 shows the critical fix: adding `left = left.delete(data, bc)` in the two-children case and adding `return this` to ensure the current node is properly returned after modification. Earlier attempts (visible in the testRemoveReturnValue diffs at runs 87-93) show different approaches to predecessor cleanup: directly reassigning `this.left`, setting `predecessor = predecessor.left`, and commenting out lines. The correct approach, implemented at run 95, is to copy the predecessor's data into the current node, then recursively call delete on the left subtree to remove the predecessor node, capturing the result back into the left pointer.
nextSteps: The two-children removal algorithm is: (1) find the in-order predecessor by going left once then right as far as possible, (2) copy the predecessor's data into the node being removed, (3) recursively delete the predecessor's key from the left subtree with `left = left.delete(predecessorData, bc)`. This same logic applies in EditorTrees Milestone 3 with the added complexity of maintaining balance codes.

The `return this` statement after modifying a node during removal is essential; without it, the parent loses its reference to the modified subtree. Every branch of the delete method must return either the current node (if it was modified in place) or a replacement node (if the current node was removed).

Test the two-children case specifically with trees where the predecessor has a left child of its own. This is the scenario that breaks naive implementations that simply unlink the predecessor without recursively cleaning up its subtree.

feedbackItems.pattern: Iterative rework of three-case removal logic
feedbackItems.explanation: This test first passed at run 30 but failed across runs 31–38. The diffs show that each revision between runs 31 and 38 restructured the three removal cases (leaf node, one child, two children) and the predecessor/max-finding logic. In run 30, the initial version used left.max() to find the predecessor. Run 31 expanded the logic with additional comments but introduced changes that caused the test to fail. Run 35 switched to a getMax() helper and simplified the leaf-node check by relying on the one-child cases to cover it implicitly. Run 37 re-added the explicit leaf-node check (returning NULL_NODE) alongside the one-child checks. Run 38 continued adjusting the same region. The test passed again starting at run 39 when the final version of the three-case logic and the getMax() helper were both in place. The pattern of failures and fixes across runs 31–38 shows multiple revisions to the same code regions, with the test stabilizing once all three cases and the recursive subtree reassignment were correct.
nextSteps: This three-case removal pattern recurs in EditorTrees Milestone 3, where delete(int pos) uses the same logic but adds AVL rebalancing; practice writing remove() from scratch with the invariant that each recursive call returns the new root of its subtree, so the parent always reassigns its child pointer.

When implementing the two-children case, treat it as two distinct operations: (1) copy the predecessor's data into the current node, (2) recursively remove the predecessor from the left subtree. Verify that step 2 uses the same remove method so all three cases are handled for the predecessor node as well.

Write small test trees by hand (e.g., a 3-node tree for each case) and trace the return values at each recursive level to confirm that NULL_NODE, the child node, or 'this' is returned correctly in each scenario.

feedbackItems.pattern: Method visibility or signature mismatch blocking automated tests
feedbackItems.explanation: Both testContainsStrings() and testContainsInts() failed from run 23 through run 41, despite manual tests passing from run 25 onward (11/11 passed). The contains() logic was functionally correct in manual testing, but the automated test class could not access the method, pointing to a visibility or method signature mismatch. The automated test class likely expected a specific method signature (e.g., public boolean contains(T item)) that did not match what was declared in the code. Both tests began passing together at run 42, confirming a single fix resolved both. This pattern, where code works in one context but not another, indicates an access modifier issue (e.g., package-private vs. public) or a parameter type mismatch.
nextSteps: The BST navigation pattern used in contains() (compare, go left or right, recurse) recurs in Exam 2's shortestWordAlongPath problem; make sure you can write this traversal fluently with proper method signatures that match the expected interface.

When implementing methods that must be called by external test classes, always verify the method is declared public and that its parameter and return types exactly match the interface or abstract class specification. A mismatch in generics (e.g., Comparable vs. the concrete type parameter) can cause the method to not be recognized as an override.
Consider using the @Override annotation on any method that implements an interface or overrides a superclass method; the compiler will flag signature mismatches immediately.

feedbackItems.pattern: Remove return value not propagated correctly through recursion
feedbackItems.explanation: Both testRemoveReturnValue() and testRemoveAdvanced() failed from run 23 through run 38 and passed together starting at run 39. The diff at run 39 shows the complete remove logic: the wrapper method calls root.remove(item, bc) (instead of root.insert), the three removal cases are all present (leaf returning NULL_NODE, one-child returning the other child, two-children using getMax to find the predecessor), and the predecessor's data is copied before recursively removing it. The key difference in earlier runs was that the return value from the recursive remove call was not being used to update the parent's child pointer, or the wrapper was calling the wrong method entirely. The boolean container (bc) parameter is used to communicate whether the element was actually found, which is essential for the return value test. The fix at run 39 ensured that both the structural removal and the return-value signaling were correct.
nextSteps: This pointer-replacement pattern (returning NULL_NODE or a child to detach/replace a subtree) recurs in EditorTrees Milestone 3 and Exam 2's pruneFullSubtreesSize3; practice the pattern of 'this.left = this.left.remove(...)' so the parent always captures the new subtree root.

When remove() must also communicate whether the element existed (for the return value), use a mutable container (like your BooleanContainer) and set it at the exact point where the match is found, before performing the structural removal. This separates the 'was it found?' concern from the 'restructure the tree' concern.
Test the two-children case specifically by removing an internal node and verifying both the tree structure (via toString or toArrayList) and the return value in the same test case.

feedbackItems.pattern: Incorrect return value from size() and cascading failures across core operations
feedbackItems.explanation: This test, along with testAddAndRawStringNoCollision, testToString, testAddDuplicate, testAddAll, testClear, testRemove, and testContains, failed from run 1 through run 14 due to interconnected bugs in the core hash set operations. The size() method returned -1 (a placeholder) instead of the actual size field, and isEmpty() did not correctly check whether size was zero. At run 15, the code was updated to return this.size from size() and to use Arrays.asList(table).isEmpty() for isEmpty(), and the toString method was rewritten to walk chains using a while loop over each bucket rather than just printing the first node. These fixes resolved the immediate failures for this group of tests. However, subsequent runs introduced regressions: at run 26, the add() method was changed to link new nodes to table[pos+1] instead of table[pos], breaking separate chaining by connecting nodes across different buckets. Run 27 attempted to fix this with a bounds-checked next index, but the fundamental error of linking to the wrong bucket persisted. At run 62, the hash position calculation was changed from Math.floorMod(stringHashCode(item), capacity) to capacity % stringHashCode(item), which reverses the operands of the modulus and produces incorrect bucket indices. Run 64 corrected the operand order to stringHashCode(item) % capacity with a manual negative-check, which restored correct behavior. The position calculation was modified multiple times across runs 26, 27, 62, and 64.
nextSteps: Solidify your understanding of separate chaining: when inserting a new node, it must link to the existing head of the same bucket (table[pos]), not to an adjacent bucket. The new node becomes the new head: table[pos] = new Node(item, table[pos]).

For mapping hash codes to bucket indices, use Math.floorMod(hashCode, capacity) rather than manual modulus with negative correction. floorMod always returns a non-negative result when the divisor is positive, eliminating an entire class of bugs.

When multiple tests fail simultaneously, identify the shared dependency (here, add() and position calculation) rather than fixing each test individually. Tracing one add() call by hand through the bucket array can reveal whether nodes land in the correct chain.

feedbackItems.pattern: Deferred rehash implementation resolved in final batch
feedbackItems.explanation: This rehash test failed from run 1 through run 14, passing in run 15. The diff for run 15 shows two changes to the add() method. The load factor check changed from `(double) size / capacity > 2` to `(size+1.0) / capacity > 2`. The original version evaluated the load factor after incrementing size; the corrected version evaluates whether adding one more element would exceed the threshold before insertion. This pre-check ensures the table is resized before the new element is placed into a bucket of the larger table. Additionally, the node insertion changed from `table[index] = newNode` to `table[index] = new Node(item, table[index])`. The original assignment overwrote the existing chain at that index; the corrected version prepends the new node to the existing chain. Both changes were necessary: without correct chaining, items would be lost during normal adds, and without the corrected load factor arithmetic, rehashing would trigger at the wrong time or fail to redistribute items into the doubled-capacity array properly.
nextSteps: This load-factor threshold arithmetic recurs in Exam 3, which asks how many adds trigger the first rehash given a specific capacity and lambda. Practice computing the exact element count that crosses the threshold: with capacity M and max load factor L, rehash triggers when size exceeds M*L, so the (M*L + 1)th unique add causes the resize.

When implementing rehash, remember that every existing element must be re-indexed against the new capacity using hashCode % newCapacity, not the old capacity. Walk through a small example (5 items, capacity 5 doubling to 10) on paper to verify items land in their correct new buckets.

The prepend-to-chain pattern (new Node(item, table[index])) is the standard O(1) insertion for separate chaining. Contrast this with the bug of assigning table[index] = newNode without linking to the old head, which silently drops all previously chained elements at that index.

drills.intro: Exam 3 Problem 4(c) asks you to reason about *when* a capacity-doubling rehash happens given M and λ. To make that reasoning testable on your own implementation, add a new method `public int rehashCount()` to StringHashSet that returns how many rehashes have occurred since construction. You'll need a private instance field that you increment exactly once each time your resize/rehash branch runs. Then paste this test into StringHashSetTest.java for a point back. The test pins down two boundary cases — before the first rehash, and right after it — so you can confirm your add()'s threshold logic is exact rather than off-by-one.
hints: Add a private int field initialized to 0 — e.g. `private int mRehashCount = 0;` — and a one-line public getter that returns it. The field tracks lifetime rehash count, not the count since the last clear().

Increment the field inside the branch that actually grows the array (your resize / rehash helper). Don't increment on every add() — only on the adds that crossed the lambda threshold and triggered a grow.

If the second assertion fails with a count of 0, your resize branch isn't running on the 11th add — re-read your threshold check. If it fails with 2, you may be calling resize from inside resize (e.g. recursive add during re-bucketing) — re-bucket directly into the new array instead of going through add().

feedbackItems.pattern: Iterator not implemented until final batch
feedbackItems.explanation: The iterator tests, including testIteratorDifferentReturns(), testIteratorNextHasNext(), testIteratorConcurrentModificationException(), and testIteratorNoSuchElementException(), all failed from run 1 through run 14 and passed together in run 15. The run 15 diff shows a 69-line addition that introduced the complete iterator infrastructure: a modCount field on the hash set, imports for ConcurrentModificationException and NoSuchElementException, and modCount increments in mutating methods (add, remove, clear). The iterator for a chained hash table requires tracking two pieces of state: the current bucket index in the table array and the current node within that bucket's linked list. The hasNext() method must skip over null or empty buckets to find the next available element, and next() must advance through the chain before moving to the next non-empty bucket. The testIteratorDifferentReturns and testIteratorNextHasNext tests verify that the iterator visits every element across all buckets exactly once, while the edge case tests verify proper exception behavior when next() is called without a remaining element or when the set is modified during iteration. All four tests passed simultaneously because they all depended on the same iterator class being implemented.
nextSteps: The hasNext()/next()/NoSuchElementException contract you implemented here applies to every iterator you will write, including for EditorTrees and graph traversals. The key pattern is: hasNext() must never modify state or throw; next() must throw NoSuchElementException when hasNext() would return false; and the iterator must traverse the entire backing structure without skipping or duplicating elements.

The modCount/expectedModCount pattern for fail-fast ConcurrentModificationException detection is structural: the collection increments modCount on every mutation (add, remove, clear), the iterator captures expectedModCount at construction time, and every call to next() compares the two values. Practice identifying which methods are "mutating" to ensure no increment is missed.

For hash table iterators specifically, make sure your bucket-scanning logic handles edge cases: tables where the first several buckets are empty, tables where all elements are in one bucket, and tables that have just been rehashed (changing which buckets are occupied).

feedbackItems.explanation: Across all four runs, testEmptyHashSet has failed consistently. This test checks that a freshly constructed StringHashSet reports size() == 0 and isEmpty() == true. The error indicates size() is returning -1 instead of 0, which means the size field is either uninitialized or initialized to -1 in the constructor. The size field must be explicitly initialized to 0 when the hash set is constructed, and the isEmpty() method should return true when size == 0. nextSteps: In your constructor, ensure the size instance variable is explicitly set to 0 and that the internal bucket array is allocated (e.g., new Node[initialCapacity]). These two initializations are the foundation every other method depends on.
Implement isEmpty() to return size == 0. This is a one-line method, but it must agree with your size field, so verify that size is only modified inside add(), remove(), and clear().

feedbackItems.pattern: Persistent incorrect size tracking
feedbackItems.explanation: testSize has failed in all four runs with size() returning -1 both before and after add operations. This is closely related to the empty-state issue: the size field starts at -1 instead of 0, and add() does not increment it. Even if add() were partially implemented, the size would remain wrong because the field was never properly initialized. The code changed between runs 1-4 across two variants, but neither addressed size initialization or size updates inside add(). Correct size tracking requires three things: initializing size to 0 in the constructor, incrementing size by 1 each time a new (non-duplicate) element is successfully added, and decrementing size by 1 each time an element is successfully removed.
nextSteps: Initialize size to 0 in the constructor. Then, inside add(), increment size only when the element is not already present in the set (i.e., after checking for duplicates and successfully inserting a new node).
Inside remove(), decrement size only when an element is actually found and removed. Inside clear(), reset size to 0.

feedbackItems.pattern: Null output from unimplemented add/toString
feedbackItems.explanation: This test has failed across all four runs, with toString and toRawString returning null. The test adds elements that hash to distinct buckets (no collisions) and then checks the raw string representation of the internal table. The null output indicates that add() is not inserting nodes into the bucket array, and toRawString() has nothing to display. The code changed between runs, but no test passes were produced. The add() method needs to: (1) compute the hash code using the polynomial 31x+y function (which is already working), (2) reduce it to a valid bucket index using Math.abs(hashCode) % capacity, (3) walk the chain at that index to check for duplicates, and (4) if no duplicate is found, prepend a new node to the chain and increment size.
nextSteps: This separate-chaining insertion pattern recurs in Exam 3 (separate chaining T/F); make sure you understand that each bucket stores either null or a reference to the head of a linked list of nodes. Implement add() by computing the bucket index, walking the existing chain to check for duplicates, and prepending a new node if the element is absent.

Implement toRawString() to iterate over every bucket index, printing null for empty buckets and the chain of node values for non-empty ones. This gives you a visual debugging tool for verifying that add() places elements in the correct buckets.
Return true from add() when a new element is inserted and false when a duplicate is detected. The inverted boolean results seen in some of your runs suggest these return values may be swapped.

drills.intro: Practice the collision-counting question that appears on Exam 3 practice. Add a public int numCollidedEntries() method to StringHashSet that returns how many added items landed in a bucket that already had at least one entry — this is exactly the per-bucket walk your toRawString does, but counting instead of formatting. hints: An entry 'collided' if it was inserted into a bucket that was already non-null at the moment of insertion. With separate chaining, that means it became the 2nd, 3rd, ... node in some chain.
Walk each bucket once. For each bucket, count nodes beyond the head: a chain of length k contributes (k - 1) collided entries; an empty bucket contributes 0; a singleton contributes 0.

feedbackItems.pattern: Null output from missing element storage
feedbackItems.explanation: testToString has failed in all four runs, receiving null instead of a bracketed, comma-separated string of elements. This failure is a direct consequence of add() not inserting elements into the bucket array. The toString() method needs to collect all elements from all non-empty buckets and format them, but if no elements are stored, there is nothing to collect. The code changed between runs, but the underlying add() implementation was not updated. Once add() correctly inserts nodes into the bucket array, toString() can be implemented by iterating through each bucket, walking each chain, collecting element values, and joining them with commas inside square brackets.
nextSteps: Focus on getting add() working first, since toString() depends entirely on elements being present in the bucket array. Once add() is functional, toString() becomes a straightforward traversal.

Implement toString() by iterating over all buckets (index 0 through capacity-1), and for each non-null bucket, walk the linked list and append each element's value to a result. Format the final output as [element1, element2, ...] with square brackets.
Handle the empty-set edge case: toString() on an empty set should return "[]" rather than null.

drills.intro: Your toString is returning null elements, likely because elements aren't being stored properly in the buckets. Let's test toString with multiple elements that land in different buckets to isolate the storage issue. Paste this into StringHashSetTest.java for a point back.
hints: Hint 1: toString iterates over all buckets and collects stored strings. If you see 'null' in the output, it means a bucket or node reference is null but you're still appending it to the result.

Hint 2: When building the string, you need to skip null buckets entirely. For each non-null bucket, walk the linked list chain and only append actual string values. Check your loop condition: are you iterating the array length or only non-null entries?

Hint 3: In your toString, before appending a node's data, verify the node itself is not null. A common bug is using a for loop like 'for (int i = 0; i < array.length; i++)' but not checking 'if (array[i] != null)' before traversing that bucket's chain.

feedbackItems.pattern: Null output from missing add and rehash logic
feedbackItems.explanation: This test has failed across all four runs. It adds enough elements to trigger a rehash (capacity doubling when the load factor exceeds the threshold) and then checks the raw string output of the resized table. Since add() is not inserting elements, the load factor never increases, rehash is never triggered, and the output is null. This test depends on multiple layers of functionality: working add(), correct size tracking, load factor computation, and the rehash procedure itself. The code changed between runs, but no progress was made on any of these layers.
nextSteps: This rehash logic appears directly on Exam 3 (minimum adds to trigger rehash, rehash diagram); understanding it deeply now will pay off. After each successful add, check if (size / capacity) exceeds your load factor threshold. If it does, allocate a new array of double the capacity, then re-insert every existing element by recomputing bucket indices against the new capacity.

Implement rehash as a separate private method. Create the new array, iterate over every chain in the old array, and for each node, compute its new bucket index using Math.abs(hashCode) % newCapacity and prepend it to the new chain. Then replace the old array with the new one and update the capacity field.

Before attempting rehash, make sure add() and size tracking are fully working. Test with a small number of elements first to confirm correct bucket placement, then increase the count past the rehash threshold and verify the raw string shows the doubled capacity.

To make that reasoning testable on your own implementation, add a new method `public int rehashCount()` to StringHashSet that returns how many rehashes have occurred since construction. You'll need a private instance field that you increment exactly once each time your resize/rehash branch runs. Then paste this test into StringHashSetTest.java for a point back. The test pins down two boundary cases — before the first rehash, and right after it — so you can confirm your add()'s threshold logic is exact rather than off-by-one.
hints: Add a private int field initialized to 0 — e.g. `private int mRehashCount = 0;` — and a one-line public getter that returns it. The field tracks lifetime rehash count, not the count since the last clear().

Increment the field inside the branch that actually grows the array (your resize / rehash helper). Don't increment on every add() — only on the adds that crossed the lambda threshold and triggered a grow.

If the second assertion fails with a count of 0, your resize branch isn't running on the 11th add — re-read your threshold check. If it fails with 2, you may be calling resize from inside resize (e.g. recursive add during re-bucketing) — re-bucket directly into the new array instead of going through add().

feedbackItems.pattern: Unimplemented fail-fast modification detection

At the start of both hasNext() and next() in your iterator, compare the set's current modCount against the iterator's expectedModCount. If they differ, throw a new ConcurrentModificationException. This single check is all that is needed to make the iterator fail-fast.

feedbackItems.pattern: Post-increment vs pre-increment confusion in iterator next()
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed across runs 24-28. In run 25, the code changed to `list.get(index++)`, which uses post-increment; this returns the current value of index and then increments it, causing the first call to return element 0 but subsequent logic produced incorrect results. In run 26, the code changed to `index += 1` followed by `return list.get(index)`, which increments before returning and skipped the first element, producing the error "expected: <1> but was: <2>". In run 28, the code used `int newindex = index++`, which assigns the old value to newindex while incrementing index. The test passed at run 25 and remained passing through run 28. The changes across these runs involved different approaches to incrementing the index relative to accessing the list element.
nextSteps: This iterator index-management pattern recurs in EditorTrees toString(), which requires an O(N) in-order traversal; practice writing next() as two clear steps: (1) capture the current element, (2) advance the index, then return the captured element, rather than combining both into one expression with increment operators.

When implementing any iterator's next(), always verify behavior on the first call (should return the first element) and the last call (should return the last element without going out of bounds). Write a small test with a 3-element list to confirm.

Prefer separating side effects from return values: use `T result = list.get(index); index++; return result;` instead of combining increment and access in a single expression, which reduces off-by-one bugs.

diffs.label: Run 28 — BinarySearchTree.java
diffs.note: Changed next() to use `int newindex = index++` with post-increment, capturing the old index for the return while advancing; this resolved the off-by-one.

This specific test validates that modifying the hash set (via add, remove, or clear) after creating an iterator causes the iterator to throw ConcurrentModificationException on subsequent calls. This is a standard fail-fast iterator pattern used throughout Java collections.
nextSteps: Add an integer modCount field to your hash set class. Increment it in every mutating method: add(), remove(), clear(), and addAll(). This counter does not need to be decremented or reset; it only needs to increase on each structural modification.

In your iterator's constructor, store the current modCount value as expectedModCount. At the start of both hasNext() and next(), check if the hash set's modCount still equals expectedModCount. If not, throw a new ConcurrentModificationException.

For testIteratorNoSuchElementException(), ensure that when hasNext() returns false and next() is called anyway, you throw NoSuchElementException. This is a separate check from the concurrent modification check and should be evaluated after the modification check passes.

feedbackItems.pattern: Unimplemented iterator returning null

It specifically validates the basic hasNext()/next() contract: that hasNext() returns true when elements remain, next() returns each element exactly once, and hasNext() returns false after all elements have been visited. The test has failed across all 33 runs because the iterator() method does not return a working Iterator. The traversal logic must handle the two-dimensional structure of the hash table: an outer loop over bucket indices and an inner traversal of each bucket's linked list chain.
nextSteps: Focus on the state machine inside your iterator: maintain a bucketIndex (int) and a currentNode (linked list node reference). When currentNode becomes null after a next() call, scan forward through the table array starting at bucketIndex+1 to find the next non-null bucket, and set currentNode to that bucket's head. If no more non-null buckets exist, currentNode stays null and hasNext() returns false.

Initialize the iterator correctly in its constructor: set bucketIndex to 0 and scan forward to the first non-null bucket, setting currentNode to that bucket's head. If the table is entirely empty, currentNode should be null from the start.

Verify that your iterator visits every element exactly once by mentally tracing through a small example: a table of capacity 4 with elements in buckets 0 and 3, each with two nodes chained. Confirm your logic transitions from the last node in bucket 0 to the first node in bucket 3.

feedbackItems.pattern: Unimplemented iterator returning null

The fix requires the same iterator implementation described for the other iterator tests, with an explicit guard in the next() method.
nextSteps: In your next() method, before doing anything else (after the concurrent modification check), call hasNext(). If it returns false, throw new NoSuchElementException(). This ensures the exception is thrown both when the set is empty and when the iterator has been fully exhausted.

feedbackItems.pattern: Persistent failure across incremental feature builds
feedbackItems.explanation: This test (testAddAndRawStringRehash) and the related testAddAndRawStringNoRehash both failed for 14 runs before passing at run 15. These tests validate the raw internal structure of the hash table, meaning they are sensitive to every detail: hash index computation, chaining order within buckets, and (for the rehash test) correct capacity doubling with redistribution. The run 15 diff reveals two critical changes applied together. First, the hash index formula changed from `Math.abs(hash) % capacity` to `(hash & 0x7fffffff) % capacity`, which avoids the edge case where `Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE)` returns a negative number, producing a negative array index. Second, the rehash loop was restructured from a for-each over the old table (`for (Node head: oldTable)`) to an explicit index-based loop (`for (int i = 0; i < oldCapacity; i++)`), with `oldCapacity` captured before the capacity field is doubled. This is necessary because the for-each approach, combined with calling `add()` internally, could produce incorrect behavior if the capacity field was already updated. The large diff (68 lines added) also included the iterator infrastructure and modification counter (`count`), but the core changes for these two tests were the hash computation and rehash loop restructuring. The fact that both the no-rehash and rehash variants failed together indicates they shared the same root cause in the add/hashing pipeline, with the rehash test additionally depending on correct redistribution logic.
nextSteps: This rehash threshold arithmetic recurs on Exam 3, which asks how many adds trigger the first rehash given a specific capacity and load factor. Practice computing ceil(capacity * loadFactor) for different table sizes to build fluency with the trigger condition and the redistribution that follows.

Understand why `(hash & 0x7fffffff) % capacity` is preferred over `Math.abs(hash) % capacity`: the bitwise mask clears the sign bit without the overflow risk of Math.abs on Integer.MIN_VALUE, guaranteeing a non-negative index for every possible hash code.

When implementing rehash, always capture the old capacity and old table reference before modifying any fields. Then iterate the old table with an index-based loop, re-inserting each node into the new (already-resized) table. This avoids subtle bugs where the capacity field has already changed mid-iteration.

feedbackItems.pattern: Unimplemented iterator returning null
feedbackItems.explanation: All four iterator-related tests, including testIteratorDifferentReturns(), testIteratorNextHasNext(), testIteratorNoSuchElementException(), and testIteratorConcurrentModificationException(), have failed across all 33 runs because the iterator() method has not been implemented and returns null. These tests collectively verify the full java.util.Iterator contract for a hash set: hasNext() and next() must traverse all elements across all non-empty buckets, next() must throw NoSuchElementException when exhausted, and mutation of the set during iteration must trigger ConcurrentModificationException. The hasNext()/next()/NoSuchElementException contract recurs in every iterator you write for hash sets, EditorTrees, graphs, and other collections, so building a solid understanding here pays off repeatedly. Since the underlying table structure and chaining are working correctly, the iterator implementation is purely a traversal layer on top of existing, functional data.
nextSteps: Create an inner class that implements Iterator<String>. It needs two pieces of state: the current index into the table array and the current Node in the chain at that index. The constructor should advance to the first non-null bucket. hasNext() returns true if the current node is non-null. next() returns the current node's data, advances to the next node in the chain, and if the chain is exhausted, scans forward through the table array to find the next non-null bucket. Throw NoSuchElementException from next() when there are no more elements.

For ConcurrentModificationException support, maintain a modCount field in the hash set that increments on every add, remove, or clear call. The iterator's constructor captures this value as expectedModCount, and each call to hasNext() or next() checks whether modCount still matches. This fail-fast pattern recurs in every mutable collection you will build, so internalizing it now is valuable.

feedbackItems.pattern: Unimplemented iterator returning null
feedbackItems.explanation: This test is part of the same group as testIteratorDifferentReturns(), testIteratorNextHasNext(), and testIteratorNoSuchElementException(), all failing because the iterator() method returns null. This specific test validates the ConcurrentModificationException (CME) behavior: after obtaining an iterator, if the set is mutated (via add or remove), subsequent calls to the iterator's next() should detect the modification and throw CME. The modCount/expectedModCount pattern that detects mutation during iteration recurs in every mutable collection you will write. The fix is structural, requiring a modCount field on the hash set class and a snapshot of that count stored in the iterator at construction time.
nextSteps: Add an int modCount field to your hash set class and increment it in every mutating method: add(), remove(), clear(), and addAll(). In your iterator's constructor, store expectedModCount = modCount. At the start of next() (and optionally hasNext()), check if modCount != expectedModCount and throw ConcurrentModificationException if they differ.
Test this by creating an iterator, then calling add() or remove() on the set, then calling next() on the iterator. The CME should fire immediately on the next iterator operation after the mutation.
Remember that rehash is called internally by add() and should not independently increment modCount beyond what add() already does, or you may get false CME triggers.

feedbackItems.explanation: This test belongs to the same group as testIteratorDifferentReturns(), testIteratorNoSuchElementException(), and testIteratorConcurrentModificationException(). All four fail because iterator() returns null. This particular test focuses on the core hasNext()/next() contract: calling hasNext() should not advance the iterator, and calling next() should return each element exactly once. The test likely adds several elements and then iterates through them, verifying that the count of returned elements matches the set's size and that hasNext() returns false only after all elements have been consumed.
nextSteps: When implementing hasNext(), ensure it is a pure query with no side effects: it should return true if the current node reference is non-null, and false otherwise. Do not advance any pointers inside hasNext().

In next(), return the current element, then advance: first try moving to the next node in the current bucket's chain. If that chain is exhausted (node becomes null), increment the table index and scan forward until you find a non-null bucket or reach the end of the table. This two-level traversal (chain within bucket, then next bucket) is the key pattern for hash table iteration.
Consider writing a small manual test: create a set, add 3-4 elements, get an iterator, and print each call to hasNext() and next() to verify the traversal visits every element exactly once.

feedbackItems.pattern: Persistent null output from unimplemented add method
feedbackItems.explanation: This test, along with testAddAndRawStringNoRehash, has failed across all 12 runs with the rawString output returning null, indicating that the add method never stores elements into the hash table's bucket array. Runs 1-5 produced changes to hash code computation, which succeeded by run 5. From run 5 through run 12, the add method itself remained unchanged. The test expects that after calling add with a string, the corresponding bucket in the internal array contains a linked list node holding that string. Since the bucket remains null, the element is not inserted. This is the root cause that cascades into nearly every other test failure in the assignment.
nextSteps: This separate chaining pattern recurs in Exam 3, where Problem 1(c) tests whether every bucket stores either a node reference or null. To implement add: (1) compute the hash code of the string, (2) take the absolute value and mod by the table capacity to get a bucket index, (3) walk the linked list at that bucket to check for duplicates, and (4) if not found, create a new node and prepend it to the chain at that index, then increment size.

After inserting the node, verify that your add method returns the correct boolean: true if the element was newly added, false if it was already present. This duplicate-detection step requires traversing the existing chain at the bucket index and comparing each node's data to the incoming string.
Test your add method in isolation before moving on: after a single add("hello"), confirm that table[hashCode("hello") % capacity] is not null and that size() returns 1.

drills.intro: Practice the collision-counting question that appears on Exam 3 practice. Add a public int numCollidedEntries() method to StringHashSet that returns how many added items landed in a bucket that already had at least one entry — this is exactly the per-bucket walk your toRawString does, but counting instead of formatting. Then paste this test into StringHashSetTest.java for a point back. The empty case is the warm-up; harder variants follow.
hints: An entry 'collided' if it was inserted into a bucket that was already non-null at the moment of insertion. With separate chaining, that means it became the 2nd, 3rd, ... node in some chain.
Walk each bucket once. For each bucket, count nodes beyond the head: a chain of length k contributes (k - 1) collided entries; an empty bucket contributes 0; a singleton contributes 0.
An empty hash set has no entries, so the count is 0. Keep the implementation O(N) — visit each entry exactly once.

feedbackItems.pattern: Persistent incorrect size due to non-functional add
feedbackItems.explanation: The size test has failed in all 12 runs. Since the add method does not store elements into the hash table, the internal size counter is never incremented. The test calls add multiple times and then checks that size() returns the correct count. Even if a size field exists and is initialized to 0, it remains 0 if add never modifies it. This test is entirely dependent on a working add method that both inserts elements and increments the size counter on successful, non-duplicate insertions.
nextSteps: Ensure that your add method increments the size field exactly once per successful insertion, only when the element is not already present in the set. A common mistake is incrementing size before checking for duplicates, which would overcount.
Also ensure that remove decrements size when an element is successfully removed, and that clear resets size to 0. Consistent bookkeeping across all mutating operations is what makes size() reliable.

nextSteps: First, get add working so that elements exist in the table. Then implement toString by iterating through the bucket array from index 0 to capacity-1, and for each non-null bucket, walking the linked list and collecting each node's string value.

feedbackItems.pattern: Persistent rehash failure due to non-functional add
feedbackItems.explanation: This test has failed in all 12 runs. It verifies that after enough elements are added to exceed the load factor threshold, the hash table doubles its capacity and redistributes all existing elements into new buckets. Since add does not insert elements, the load factor never increases, rehash is never triggered, and the test fails. Rehash depends on a fully working add method that both inserts elements and checks the load factor after each insertion.
nextSteps: This rehash logic recurs in Exam 3, where Problem 4(c)(ii) asks how many adds trigger the first rehash given a specific capacity and load factor threshold. After each successful add, compute the current load factor (size / capacity) and compare it to your threshold. If it meets or exceeds the threshold, allocate a new array of double the capacity, then re-insert every element from the old table by recomputing bucket indices against the new capacity.

During rehash, do not simply copy bucket references from the old array to the new one. Each element must be re-hashed because the bucket index depends on capacity (hash % newCapacity), so elements that shared a bucket before may land in different buckets after doubling.
After rehash completes, verify that size remains unchanged (you are redistributing, not adding new elements) and that the new capacity is exactly double the old one.

feedbackItems.pattern: Regression from negative hash index
feedbackItems.explanation: This test first passed at run 3 after the initial implementation of the hash set's core fields (size, Node array, version) and basic add/contains/remove logic (127 lines added). It regressed at run 6 due to an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException with index -1, which occurred because the polynomial hash function was producing negative values that were used directly as array indices. The fix at run 6 introduced a stringHashIndex helper method that attempted to handle negative hashes by adding Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1, but this approach had an overflow issue. Run 7 refined the helper to conditionally add Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 only when the hash is negative, which resolved the regression. The root cause was that Java's modulo operator (%) preserves the sign of the dividend, so a negative hash code modded by the array length yields a negative index. The test passed from run 7 onward.
nextSteps: Understand that Java's % operator is a remainder, not a true modulus: when the dividend is negative, the result is negative. The standard fix is to use Math.floorMod(hash, array.length) or to mask with & 0x7FFFFFFF before taking %. Adding Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 to a negative int can itself overflow, so prefer bitwise masking.

When writing any hash-based data structure, always centralize index computation in a single helper method (as you eventually did with stringHashIndex) so that every operation, including add, contains, remove, and rehash, uses the same safe mapping from hash code to bucket index.
Write a quick unit test with strings whose polynomial hash codes are negative to catch sign-related index bugs early, before they cascade into multiple test failures.

feedbackItems.explanation: The iterator tests, including testIteratorDifferentReturns, testIteratorNextHasNext, testIteratorNoSuchElementException, and testIteratorConcurrentModificationException, have all been failing since run 1 with no implementation attempts across 23 runs. These four tests collectively validate the full Iterator contract for a hash set: hasNext() must correctly detect remaining elements, next() must return each element exactly once across all buckets, next() must throw NoSuchElementException when exhausted, and structural modifications to the set must trigger ConcurrentModificationException. This java.util.Iterator contract recurs in future assignments (EditorTrees, graphs), so building a solid understanding now is important.
nextSteps: This Iterator contract pattern recurs in every mutable collection you will build. Implement a custom inner class that implements Iterator<String>. It needs two pieces of state: (1) the current bucket index in the array, and (2) the current node within that bucket's chain. In the constructor, advance to the first non-null bucket. hasNext() returns true if the current node is non-null. next() returns the current node's value, advances to the next node in the chain, and if the chain is exhausted, scans forward to the next non-null bucket.

For fail-fast behavior, maintain a modCount field in the hash set that increments on every add, remove, or clear. When creating the iterator, snapshot modCount into an expectedModCount field. At the start of each next() call, compare the two; if they differ, throw ConcurrentModificationException. This is the standard pattern used in Java's own collections.

For the NoSuchElementException case, check hasNext() at the beginning of next(). If hasNext() is false, throw NoSuchElementException before doing anything else. This ensures the iterator signals exhaustion correctly.

feedbackItems.pattern: Missing remove implementation resolved in batch
feedbackItems.explanation: Both testRemove() and testRemoveAdvanced() (along with testRemoveReturnValue()) failed from run 5 through run 16, then all passed together at run 17. The diff for run 17 shows 50 lines added, including a new Node.remove(T item) method with a NULL_NODE base case and a Box helper class for communicating the removed value back to the caller. The remove operation in a BST requires handling three cases: removing a leaf (return NULL_NODE), removing a node with one child (return that child), and removing a node with two children (replace with the in-order successor, then recursively remove the successor from the right subtree). The Box class pattern allows returning both the modified subtree and a value indicating whether the removal succeeded, since Java methods can only return one value. The testRemoveAdvanced() test exercises the two-children case and deeper tree structures, while testRemoveReturnValue() verifies that remove() correctly reports whether an element was actually found and removed.
nextSteps: The three-case BST removal logic recurs directly in EditorTrees Milestone 3, where delete(int pos) applies the same leaf/one-child/two-children cases but adds AVL rebalancing on the way back up the recursion; make sure you can identify which case applies and how pointer reassignment works in each.

Practice the 'return the new subtree root' pattern: each recursive call to remove() should return the (possibly changed) root of that subtree, and the parent must assign it back (e.g., this.left = this.left.remove(item)). This pointer-replacement pattern also appears in pruning problems on Exam 2.

For the two-children case, understand why you find the in-order successor (leftmost node in the right subtree), copy its data into the current node, and then remove the successor from the right subtree. This avoids restructuring the entire tree.

feedbackItems.pattern: Missing recursive contains helper, incorrect null sentinel comparison
feedbackItems.explanation: Both testContainsStrings() and testContainsInts() failed from run 20 through run 34, requiring 15 runs to resolve. The contains() method was initially stubbed to simply return false, which meant every lookup failed regardless of tree contents. The code diff at run 35 shows two key changes: first, the isEmpty() check was corrected from `root==null` to `root==NULL_NODE` (which had already been fixed in run 34 for isEmpty itself but was also present in the contains path), and second, a proper recursive helper method `contains(T item, Node n)` was introduced. This helper follows the standard BST search pattern: check for NULL_NODE as the base case (return false), then compare the item against the current node's data to decide whether to recurse left or right. Before this change, the public contains() method had no recursive traversal logic at all. The fix replaced the hardcoded `return false` with a delegation to the new recursive helper, which correctly navigates the tree structure using comparisons.
nextSteps: The BST search pattern (compare, go left or right, base case at null) recurs directly in Exam 2's shortestWordAlongPath, which navigates the tree the same way but accumulates data along the path. Practice writing this navigation pattern from scratch to build fluency.

When implementing recursive BST methods, always start by defining the base case (reaching NULL_NODE) and the recursive case (comparing the item to the current node's data to choose left or right). This three-way branching structure is the foundation of nearly every BST operation.

Be mindful of which sentinel value your tree uses. If your BST uses a NULL_NODE sentinel instead of Java null, every comparison in every method must use NULL_NODE consistently; mixing the two causes subtle bugs like the one in isEmpty() that cascaded here.
