feedbackItems.pattern: Incorrect null sentinel comparison in isEmpty()
feedbackItems.explanation: testIsEmpty() failed from run 20 through run 33, taking 14 runs to resolve. The root cause was a single-character-level bug: isEmpty() compared `root==null` instead of `root==NULL_NODE`. When a BST implementation uses a NULL_NODE sentinel object (a special static node instance representing empty subtrees), the root of an empty tree is set to NULL_NODE, not Java's null. Comparing against null would always return false, making isEmpty() report that the tree was never empty. The fix at run 34 was a one-line change, swapping `root==null` to `root==NULL_NODE`. This is a common pitfall when using the null-object pattern in tree implementations. The fact that this bug persisted for 14 runs, including a stall period from runs 30-32 with no code changes, preceded the correction.
nextSteps: The null-object pattern (NULL_NODE) is used extensively in EditorTrees, where rank computation depends on size queries that must correctly identify empty subtrees. Internalize the rule: if your tree uses a sentinel, every emptiness check in every method must compare against that sentinel, never against Java null.

When debugging a persistent failure, check all methods that test for emptiness or leaf status. A sentinel mismatch in one method (like isEmpty) can cause cascading failures in tests for other operations that depend on it.
Consider adding an assertion or comment at the top of your BST class documenting which sentinel convention you use, so you catch mismatches during code review.

feedbackItems.pattern: Missing ConcurrentModificationException for addAll mutation
feedbackItems.explanation: This test has failed across all 14 runs, making it the only remaining failing test in the implementation. The test checks that mutating the hash set during iteration throws a ConcurrentModificationException (CME). The standard fail-fast pattern requires a modCount field on the collection that is incremented on every structural modification (add, remove, clear, addAll), and an expectedModCount field in the iterator that is set to modCount at construction time. On each call to hasNext() or next(), the iterator compares expectedModCount to modCount and throws CME if they differ. The run 13 diff shows the iterator tracks expectedSize and throws CME when expectedSize != size, but this approach has a limitation: the addAll() method likely increments size by the same amount as the number of elements added, yet if it does not also trigger the CME detection mechanism properly, or if the check only runs in next() but not in the right place, the test will miss the mutation. Additionally, using size comparison instead of a dedicated modCount can fail when an addAll followed by a remove leaves size unchanged, making the pattern fundamentally fragile. Across all 14 runs, the addAll() method has not been connected to the modification-tracking mechanism.
nextSteps: The modCount/expectedModCount pattern recurs in every mutable collection you will write, including EditorTrees and graph structures. Replace your size-based comparison with a dedicated modCount integer field: increment modCount in every method that structurally modifies the set (add, remove, clear, and addAll). In your iterator constructor, capture expectedModCount = modCount, then check expectedModCount != modCount at the start of both hasNext() and next().

Verify that addAll() increments modCount for each successful insertion, or at minimum once if any insertion occurs. The key insight is that addAll delegates to add(), so if add() already increments modCount, addAll will naturally trigger CME detection without extra code.

Test your fix by creating an iterator, then calling addAll on the set, then calling next() on the iterator; the CME should fire immediately. Also verify that creating a new iterator after addAll works normally, since the new iterator captures the updated modCount.

feedbackItems.pattern: Regression from division-vs-modulo reintroduction
feedbackItems.explanation: This test, along with testAddAndRawStringNoRehash, testAddDuplicate, and testClear, first passed at run 3 when the hash index computation was corrected from division (hash/cap) to modulo (hash%cap). All four tests then regressed at run 6, where an 85-line change was made that included iterator and other functionality. The run 6 diff shows the division-to-modulo bug reappearing in one code path, indicating the code was restructured in a way that reintroduced the hash/cap bug. By run 7, a similar-sized change restored the modulo operation and all four tests passed again. The root cause in both the original failure and the regression was using integer division instead of modulo to map hash codes to bucket indices, which produces indices outside the valid array range or maps to incorrect buckets.
nextSteps: When restructuring code, keep the bucket-index computation (Math.abs(hashCode) % capacity) isolated in a single helper method so it cannot accidentally be duplicated with the wrong operator. This same per-bucket indexing pattern appears in exam problems about separate chaining, where you must identify which bucket an element lands in.
Before committing large refactors, run the full test suite to catch regressions immediately. The 4-test regression at run 6 could have been caught before adding more code on top.
Remember that hash % capacity gives a value in [0, capacity), while hash / capacity gives an unpredictable quotient. This distinction is fundamental to all hash table implementations.

feedbackItems.pattern: Persistent rehash failure due to hardcoded initial capacity
feedbackItems.explanation: This rehash test failed for 12 consecutive runs before passing at run 13. Early failures (runs 1-2) were ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException from the division-vs-modulo bug. After that was fixed in run 3, the rehash test continued to fail with an IndexOutOfBoundsException specific to the rehash path (Index 5 out of bounds for length 5), indicating the table was not actually growing. The test likely uses a constructor with a custom initial capacity, but the initialize() method was hardcoding DEFAULT_CAPACITY for both the array allocation and the cap field. The run 13 diff shows the fix: changing `set = new Node[DEFAULT_CAPACITY]` to `set = new Node[initialCapacity]` and `cap = DEFAULT_CAPACITY` to `cap = initialCapacity`. This meant that even after checkRehash() called initialize(cap*2), the new table was still created at the default size, so elements would hash to indices beyond the array bounds. The fix ensured that the capacity parameter actually propagated through initialization.
nextSteps: When implementing rehash, the doubled capacity must flow through every step: allocate the new array at 2*oldCapacity, update the capacity field, then re-insert every element using the new capacity for index computation. Exam problems on rehashing (such as diagramming re-bucketing after a capacity doubling) test exactly this chain of updates.
Avoid hardcoding constants like DEFAULT_CAPACITY in methods that serve dual purposes (initial construction and rehash reinitialization). Use a parameterized helper so the capacity is always explicit.

Verify your load factor threshold arithmetic: with a load factor limit of 2 and initial capacity 5, rehash should trigger when size exceeds 10. Trace through the exact add count that triggers rehash and confirm the new capacity is 10.

feedbackItems.pattern: Regression from incorrect pointer reassignment in remove
feedbackItems.explanation: This test, along with testRemove, covers the core remove operation and its return value. The test first failed at run 45 when the initial remove implementation was added, then passed at run 51 when the remove method was changed to capture the return value of removeHelper, replacing a pattern that created a new root node and called removeHelper without using its return. The test regressed at run 54 when further changes to handle the two-child removal case reintroduced failures; the remove logic produced incorrect values (expected 14 but got 4), indicating the in-order successor lookup was not correctly replacing the deleted node's data or reconnecting subtrees. The fix at run 55 rewrote the two-child case with a proper loop to find the in-order successor, tracking a 'prev' pointer and using comparisons to walk right through the left subtree. Across all these changes, the pattern that emerged was that removeHelper must return the (possibly updated) subtree root at every recursive call, and the caller must always reassign its child pointer to that returned value.
nextSteps: The three-case removal pattern (leaf, one child, two children via in-order successor) recurs directly in EditorTrees Milestone 3 delete(int pos), which adds AVL rebalancing on top. Practice writing remove so that each recursive call returns the new subtree root, letting the parent automatically update its child pointer without special-casing.

For the two-child case specifically, drill the algorithm: go to the left subtree, walk all the way right to find the in-order predecessor (or go right then all the way left for the in-order successor), copy that node's data into the node being removed, then recursively delete the predecessor/successor node. Ensure size is decremented exactly once.

When debugging tree mutations, draw the tree state before and after each operation and verify that every parent-child link is correctly updated. The pattern of returning the modified subtree root from a helper method eliminates many pointer bugs.

feedbackItems.pattern: Persistent traversal-order and null-return errors in stack-based in-order iterator
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed across runs 26 through 39, then passed at run 40. The initial implementation at run 26 threw a NullPointerException during Stack initialization, likely from not properly handling the NULL_NODE sentinel. At run 27, the NPE was resolved but the traversal order was incorrect (returned 1 instead of 2), indicating the iterator was not correctly pushing left children before returning values. At run 28, a change broke 10 other tests, indicating a modification to shared tree structure or the Node class. After recovery at run 29, the iterator returned null instead of a value, meaning next() was falling through without returning the popped node's data. The fix at run 40 involved changing the flag value pushed onto the auxiliary flags stack from 1 to 2 and adding logic to handle revisiting a node: after popping a node, if it has a right child, the right child is pushed with flag 1 (first visit), while the current node's data is returned. This dual-stack approach (one for nodes, one for visit-state flags) correctly implements in-order traversal by tracking whether a node's left subtree has already been explored.
nextSteps: The in-order iterator pattern directly parallels EditorTrees toString(), which must traverse a rank-ordered tree in O(N). Solidify your understanding of the standard stack-based in-order algorithm: push the current node onto the stack, go left until you hit NULL_NODE, then pop, return that node's data, and move to its right child. This avoids the complexity of a flags stack entirely.

Compare your dual-stack (node + flags) approach with the simpler single-stack approach where you always push-left on entry and after processing a right child. The single-stack version has fewer edge cases and is less error-prone.

Test your iterator on small trees (e.g., a three-node tree with root, left, right) by hand-tracing the stack contents at each call to next(). Verify the output matches the expected in-order sequence before running automated tests.

feedbackItems.pattern: Incorrect boolean logic in exhaustive tree search
feedbackItems.explanation: This test checks containsNonBST, which must search the entire tree (not using BST ordering) to find a value. The test failed from run 1 through run 8, consistently returning false when it should have returned true. The initial implementation compiled at run 3 but had incorrect logic; runs 4 through 8 showed no code changes. The fix at run 9 added 20 lines including the containsNonBST method body. The issue was that the recursive search was not correctly combining results from left and right subtrees; containsNonBST must return true if the current node matches OR if either subtree contains the value. A common pattern in failed implementations is to check only one subtree or to use AND instead of OR when combining recursive results.
nextSteps: The navigation pattern in containsNonBST generalizes to problems like shortestWordAlongPath on Exam 2, where you traverse based on BST ordering but accumulate information along the path. Understand the difference: contains uses BST property to go left or right, while containsNonBST must explore both subtrees since ordering is not guaranteed.

For any exhaustive tree search, the recursive pattern is: check the current node, then return (currentMatch OR recurse(left) OR recurse(right)). Make sure your base case returns false for NULL_NODE, and that you short-circuit with true as soon as a match is found.

feedbackItems.pattern: Two-child removal case producing incorrect tree structure
feedbackItems.explanation: This test exercises the most complex removal scenario: removing a node with two children, which requires finding the in-order successor (or predecessor) and restructuring the tree. The test failed from run 45 through run 54, a span of 10 runs. While testRemove and testRemoveReturnValue passed at run 51 after correctly returning the subtree root from removeHelper, testRemoveAdvanced continued to fail with 'expected 3 but got 2' at runs 51 through 54, indicating the two-child case was not correctly replacing the removed node's data with its successor's data or was not properly detaching the successor from its original position. The fix at run 55 rewrote the successor-finding logic: it introduced a 'prev' pointer to track the parent of the successor node, used a while loop walking right through the left subtree (with a compareTo check), and added a conditional branch for when the successor is not the immediate left child. This correctly handles the case where the in-order predecessor is several levels deep in the left subtree.
nextSteps: In EditorTrees Milestone 3, delete(int pos) uses this same three-case logic but must also update balance codes and trigger rotations as the recursion unwinds. Make sure you can implement the two-child case cleanly: copy the successor's data into the node being deleted, then recursively remove the successor node (which is guaranteed to have at most one child).

A cleaner approach to the two-child case avoids manual pointer tracking: after copying the in-order successor's value into the current node, call removeHelper recursively on the appropriate subtree to delete the successor. This reduces the two-child case to a one-child or leaf case, which you already handle correctly.

When the successor is the immediate left child versus deeper in the subtree, the pointer updates differ. Draw both scenarios and verify your code handles each. The recursive approach mentioned above eliminates this distinction entirely.

feedbackItems.pattern: Incorrect stack initialization and child-push ordering in pre-order iterator
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed across runs 19 through 24, then passed at run 25. The initial implementation at run 19 failed on hasNext(), indicating the stack was not properly initialized with the root node. At run 21, the error changed to 'expected true but got false', showing hasNext() was returning incorrect results, possibly because the root was pushed unconditionally even when the tree was empty. At run 22, a NullPointerException appeared, likely from popping an empty stack or accessing a null node's children. At run 23, a broader regression broke 9 tests, indicating changes to shared infrastructure (possibly the Node class or tree fields). The fix at run 25 added 25 lines including a guard that only pushes the root if it is not NULL_NODE, stored a version field for concurrent modification detection, and kept a reference to the BinarySearchTree. The pre-order algorithm itself requires pushing right then left children (so left is processed first), and the fix ensured this ordering along with proper null-sentinel checks.
nextSteps: Pre-order traversal understanding is tested directly on Exam 3 and the Final, and is needed for HW6's preOrderInOrderBuild. The stack-based pre-order algorithm is: pop the top node, return its data, then push its right child followed by its left child (both only if not NULL_NODE). This naturally produces root-left-right order.

Always guard your iterator initialization: if the tree is empty (root == NULL_NODE), do not push anything onto the stack. This ensures hasNext() returns false immediately for empty trees, avoiding both incorrect true returns and NullPointerExceptions.

The version field you added enables fail-fast behavior if the tree is modified during iteration. This is a good practice; make sure you increment the tree's version counter in insert and remove, and check it at the start of each next() call.

feedbackItems.pattern: Iterative trial-and-error on string formatting
feedbackItems.explanation: This test directly validates the toString() output format and failed across 12 runs due to incorrect comma-separator formatting. From run 10 onward, the code attempted to build the string manually by concatenating "[" with root.toString().trim() and "]", but this approach produced various incorrect patterns over multiple iterations: missing commas, spaces before commas, trailing commas, or empty output. The core difficulty was that the recursive node-level toString() had to produce elements separated by exactly ", " with no leading or trailing separators, which is notoriously tricky to get right in a recursive in-order traversal. The solution in run 23 sidestepped this entirely by delegating to this.toArrayList().toString(), reusing Java's ArrayList formatting. While this is a valid and clean approach, the underlying skill of building formatted output from a recursive traversal is important. EditorTrees toString() is graded for O(N) efficiency and uses the same in-order collection pattern.
nextSteps: For EditorTrees toString(), which is graded on O(N) efficiency, practice building strings via StringBuilder during an in-order traversal; use a separator flag or check for the first element to avoid leading/trailing commas rather than relying on trim().

Understand why delegating to toArrayList().toString() works: ArrayList.toString() produces exactly the "[e1, e2, e3]" format, so if your toArrayList() is correct, toString() is automatically correct. This is a useful composition pattern.

When debugging formatting issues, compare your actual output character-by-character against the expected output using a debugger or print statement; subtle whitespace differences are hard to spot visually.

drills.intro: Add sproutToDepth(int d) to BinarySearchTree.java so that every null child slot of any pre-existing node at depth < d is replaced with a new node whose value equals its parent's value. Only existing nodes are visited — newly sprouted nodes do not themselves sprout children. Special case: calling sproutToDepth(0) on an empty tree creates a root with value 0. This is a 2020-21 practice Exam 2 question combining full-tree structural modification with a depth parameter. Paste this test into BSTTesting.java for a point back.
hints: Write a recursive helper sproutHelper(node, currentDepth, targetDepth): if node is NULL_NODE or currentDepth >= targetDepth, return immediately — there is nothing to sprout.

At each existing node, check the left child: if it is NULL_NODE, create new BinaryNode(node.data) and assign it (do NOT recurse into it); if it is not NULL_NODE, recurse into it with currentDepth+1. Do the same for right.
The public method handles the empty-tree special case: if targetDepth >= 0 and root == NULL_NODE, set root = new BinaryNode(0). Otherwise call sproutHelper(root, 0, targetDepth).

feedbackItems.pattern: StackOverflowError from broken iterator bucket traversal
feedbackItems.explanation: The toString test failed across all 8 runs (runs 1-8) before passing in run 9. The test threw a StackOverflowError, which originated in the iterator's advance-to-next-element logic. The original code contained a contradictory condition: `if(currentNode.next == null)` as an outer check, followed by `if(currentNode.next != null)` inside it, making the inner branch unreachable. Additionally, `currentBucket++` appeared twice without proper null guards, causing the iterator to skip buckets or fail to terminate. In run 9, the fix restructured the logic to check `currentNode != null && currentNode.next != null` for chain traversal within a bucket, and separately handled bucket increment with a null guard on `currentNode`. This eliminated the infinite loop and allowed toString to correctly iterate and format all elements.
nextSteps: When writing iterator advance logic for a hash table, always handle two distinct transitions separately: (1) moving to the next node within the same bucket's chain, and (2) moving to the first node of the next non-empty bucket. Mixing these into nested conditionals with contradictory guards is a common source of infinite loops.

Before dereferencing any node reference (e.g., currentNode.next), always check that the reference itself is non-null. This defensive null-checking pattern prevents NullPointerException and is especially important in sparse data structures like hash tables where many buckets are null.

When toString depends on an iterator, test the iterator independently first. If the iterator has a bug like an infinite loop, toString will amplify it into a StackOverflowError, making the root cause harder to diagnose.

diffs.note: Restructured the iterator's advance method to separate chain traversal (currentNode.next) from bucket advancement (currentBucket++), adding null guards on currentNode that eliminated the infinite loop causing StackOverflowError in toString.

feedbackItems.pattern: NullPointerException from unguarded node dereference in iterator
feedbackItems.explanation: This test, along with testIteratorNextHasNext, testIteratorConcurrentModificationException, and testIteratorNoSuchElementException, all failed for 8 consecutive runs (runs 1-8) due to the same bug in the iterator's bucket traversal logic. The iterator was first attempted in run 3, but the advance logic contained a critical flaw: the outer condition `if(currentNode.next == null)` would enter a block that then checked `if(currentNode.next != null)`, a logically impossible branch, so the chain-following code was unreachable. Meanwhile, `currentBucket++` was called unconditionally and duplicated, causing the iterator to skip past valid buckets or dereference null nodes. This produced NullPointerException when the iterator tried to access `currentNode.next` on a null reference, and the broken traversal also caused the StackOverflowError seen in toString. Runs 3 through 8 showed no change in test outcomes, indicating the same flawed logic persisted. In run 9, the fix added a proper null guard (`currentNode != null && currentNode.next != null`) for chain traversal and conditionally incremented `currentBucket` only when `currentNode` was non-null, correctly separating intra-bucket and inter-bucket movement. This resolved all four iterator-related tests simultaneously.
nextSteps: The java.util.Iterator contract (hasNext/next/NoSuchElementException) recurs in every collection you implement, including EditorTrees and graphs. Practice writing the advance logic as a clear state machine: after returning a value, first try to follow the chain in the current bucket; if exhausted, scan forward through buckets until a non-null head is found or the table ends.

The ConcurrentModificationException / fail-fast iterator pattern using modCount and expectedModCount is structural and reappears in every mutable collection. Make sure your iterator captures expectedModCount at construction time and checks it at the start of every next() call, independent of the traversal logic.

When multiple tests fail with the same stack trace pointing to the same method, focus debugging effort on that single method rather than trying to fix tests individually. In this case, all five failures traced back to the same advance/next logic in the iterator.

feedbackItems.pattern: Deferred implementation resolved in single batch
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed for 13 consecutive runs because no iterator implementation existed; the iterator() method returned null. At run 14, the full iterator inner class was added, including the ConcurrentModificationException detection mechanism. The implementation introduced a modCount field on StringHashSet that is incremented on every structural modification (add, remove, clear). The iterator captures this value as expectedModCount at construction time and checks it at the beginning of hasNext() and next(). If the values diverge, meaning the collection was mutated after the iterator was created, a ConcurrentModificationException is thrown. This is the standard fail-fast iterator pattern from java.util.AbstractList and HashMap. The ConcurrentModificationException/fail-fast pattern recurs in every mutable collection you will implement; understanding that it is a structural safeguard (not a concurrency lock) is important for future work.
nextSteps: The ConcurrentModificationException pattern is structural, not a one-off fix. Ensure every method that changes the hash set's logical contents (add, remove, clear, and rehash if it changes size) increments modCount. feedbackItems.pattern: Deferred implementation resolved in single batch
feedbackItems.explanation: This test failed for 13 runs because the iterator() method returned null, so any call to hasNext() or next() produced a NullPointerException. At run 14, the complete iterator was implemented with proper bucket-and-chain traversal logic. The hasNext() method must scan forward from the current position (current node in the current bucket, then subsequent buckets) to determine if any elements remain. The next() method must return the current element's data, then advance the internal pointer: first to the next node in the chain, and if that chain is exhausted, to the first non-null entry in a subsequent bucket. This two-level traversal is the defining challenge of iterating over a separate-chaining hash table. The java.util.Iterator contract (hasNext/next/NoSuchElementException) recurs in every collection you build, including EditorTrees and graph traversals.
nextSteps: To iterate a separate-chaining hash set correctly, initialize the iterator by scanning from bucket 0 to find the first non-null entry. Store both the bucket index and the node pointer. In next(), save the current node's data, advance to node.next, and if node.next is null, scan forward through buckets to find the next chain head.

Ensure hasNext() is idempotent: calling it multiple times without calling next() should always return the same result and should not advance any internal state. A common mistake is advancing the bucket index inside hasNext(), which causes elements to be skipped.

Test your iterator on edge cases: an empty set (hasNext returns false immediately), a set where all elements hash to the same bucket (single chain traversal), and a set with elements spread across many buckets (multi-bucket traversal).

feedbackItems.explanation: The tests testRemove(), testRemoveAdvanced(), testRemoveReturnValue(), and testRemoveIllegalArgumentException() all failed from run 3 through run 15 because the remove() method was not yet implemented. Early runs (3-4) had compilation issues that prevented execution entirely. From run 5 onward, other methods (insert, toArray, toArrayList, iterators) were added while remove() remained unimplemented. In run 16, a 67-line addition implemented both the in-order iterator and the remove logic together, which resolved all four tests simultaneously. The remove() method handles three distinct cases: removing a leaf node (replace with NULL_NODE), removing a node with one child (replace with that child), and removing a node with two children (find the in-order successor, copy its data, then recursively remove the successor). The recursive helper returns the updated subtree root so that the parent's child pointer is correctly reassigned. All four tests, including the edge case for IllegalArgumentException on null input, passed on the first implementation attempt in run 16.
nextSteps: The three-case BST removal pattern (leaf, one child, two children via in-order successor) recurs directly in EditorTrees Milestone 3, where delete(int pos) applies the same logic but also triggers AVL rebalancing on the way back up the recursion. Practice tracing the two-children case carefully: find the in-order successor (leftmost node in the right subtree), swap its data into the current node, then recursively remove the successor from the right subtree.

Understand why the recursive remove helper must return the (possibly updated) node reference: when a node is deleted, its parent needs to update its left or right pointer. This pointer-replacement pattern, where returning NULL_NODE detaches a subtree, appears again in Exam 2's pruneFullSubtreesSize3 problem.

For the IllegalArgumentException edge case, ensure that null-checking happens at the public method level before any recursive traversal begins. This separation of validation from recursion is a clean pattern to apply consistently across tree operations.

feedbackItems.pattern: Unimplemented method, resolved after incremental build-up
feedbackItems.explanation: The in-order iterator test failed from run 3 through run 14, then passed at run 15 when a 31-line addition introduced the InOrderIterator inner class. Early runs (3-4) failed due to compilation issues, and runs 5-14 focused on implementing other methods (insert, toArray, toArrayList, inefficientIterator, preOrderIterator). The iterator implementation uses a stack-based approach: the constructor pushes all left-spine nodes onto the stack, and each call to next() pops the top node, returns its value, then pushes the left spine of that node's right child. This is the standard O(h) space, O(n) total time in-order traversal without recursion. The implementation passed on the first attempt in run 15.
nextSteps: The stack-based in-order traversal pattern directly parallels EditorTrees toString(), which must run in O(N) via in-order traversal. Solidify your understanding of why pushing the left spine simulates the recursive call stack: each stack frame represents a node whose left subtree has been fully visited but whose own value and right subtree remain.

Practice converting between recursive and iterative tree traversals for all three orders (in-order, pre-order, post-order). Exam 3 and the Final list traversals and iterators as explicit topics, and understanding the stack-based approach for each order will help you predict traversal outputs and implement them efficiently.

Verify that your iterator correctly handles hasNext() by checking whether the stack is empty, and that it throws NoSuchElementException when next() is called on an exhausted iterator. These edge cases are easy to overlook but important for correctness.
